passages.text: WIND, a current or stream of air, moving from one place to another.
The general cause of winds is heat, which, rarefying the air in one place, makes it lighter, so that the colder and heavier air around rushes in to restore the balance.
Many of the ancients held the winds to be exhalations from the earth; and sudden gusts may well arise in this manner, from vapours bursting out of caverns.

Dr Halley explained the trade winds, which blow constantly from the east between the tropics, by the heat of the sun, which rarefies the air most where it is vertical; and as the sun moves daily westward, the air is drawn after it.
Mr Hadley afterwards showed that the easterly direction of these winds arises from the rotation of the earth, the air coming from the poles having less motion eastward than the earth at the equator.
In the Indian seas the monsoons blow one half of the year from one quarter, and the other half from the opposite, changing with the seasons.
Out of the tropics the winds are so changeable that they seem to follow no regular laws, and it is not to be expected that they can ever be foretold.
Wind is the natural movement of air or other gases relative to the surface of a planet.
Wind is caused by differences in air pressure. These differences come mainly from uneven heating of the Earth's surface by the Sun, and air flows from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure.
The trade winds are part of the Hadley circulation, named after George Hadley, who in 1735 used the rotation of the Earth to explain why these winds blow from the east.
Because of the Coriolis effect of the Earth's rotation, moving air turns to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
Monsoons are seasonal winds that change direction because land and sea heat up at different rates. They bring the rainy season to South Asia.
Meteorologists forecast wind days in advance with weather observations and computer models of the atmosphere.
Jet streams are narrow bands of strong wind high in the atmosphere, near the tropopause, which blow mainly from west to east.

reasons: Rare terms appear in both: trade winds, Hadley, monsoons, rotation of the earth.
Trade winds scores well but covers only one kind of wind.

alignments.label: Air in motion

britannica.quote: a current or stream of air

alignments.note: The same definition in new words.

alignments.label: Heat as the cause

britannica.quote: heat, which, rarefying the air in one place, makes it lighter

wikipedia.quote: uneven heating of the Earth's surface by the Sun

alignments.note: The 1797 cause holds. Wikipedia speaks of air pressure where the entry speaks of light and heavy air. This is a change in language.

alignments.label: Exhalations from the earth

britannica.quote: sudden gusts may well arise in this manner, from vapours bursting out of caverns

wikipedia.quote: air flows from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure

alignments.note: The entry still allows the ancient idea for sudden gusts. Gusts too come from air pressure and air movement, not from vapours out of the ground.

alignments.label: Halley's trade winds

britannica.quote: as the sun moves daily westward, the air is drawn after it

wikipedia.quote: used the rotation of the Earth to explain why these winds blow from the east

alignments.note: Halley was right that the sun's heat at the equator drives the trade winds. His reason for the east direction was wrong, and Hadley replaced it.

alignments.label: Hadley and rotation

britannica.quote: the easterly direction of these winds arises from the rotation of the earth

alignments.note: Hadley's explanation holds. Wikipedia names the whole tropical air circulation after him.

alignments.label: Seasonal monsoons

britannica.quote: the monsoons blow one half of the year from one quarter

wikipedia.quote: Monsoons are seasonal winds that change direction

alignments.note: The observation holds. Wikipedia adds the cause: land and sea heat at different rates.

alignments.label: Winds cannot be foretold

britannica.quote: it is not to be expected that they can ever be foretold

wikipedia.quote: Meteorologists forecast wind days in advance

alignments.note: Weather maps, the telegraph and later computers made forecasts possible. This is a change in knowledge.

alignments.label: Coriolis effect

wikipedia.quote: moving air turns to the right in the Northern Hemisphere

alignments.note: The 1797 entry uses the rotation of the earth only for the trade winds. Wikipedia applies the Coriolis effect to all large winds.

alignments.label: Jet streams

wikipedia.quote: narrow bands of strong wind high in the atmosphere

alignments.note: The 1797 entry knows only winds near the ground. Jet streams were found in the 20th century.

suggestedQuestions: How did the 1797 entry explain the trade winds?
Was the 1797 entry right that winds cannot be predicted?

How did the 1797 entry explain the trade.answer: It gives two steps. Halley explained them by the sun's heat at the equator, and thought the air followed the sun westward [B4]. Hadley then showed that the east direction comes from the rotation of the earth [B5]. Wikipedia keeps Hadley's explanation and names the Hadley circulation after him [W3].

Was the 1797 entry right that winds cann.answer: No. It said winds outside the tropics follow no regular laws and can never be foretold [B7]. Wikipedia says meteorologists now forecast wind days ahead with observations and computer models [W6].
